data.question_title: If a set \(\textit{A }\)has \(\textit{n }\) elements, then the total number of subsets of \(\textit{A }\) is
data.explanation_txt:
Let the set with \(n\) elements be:

\( A = \{ a_1,a_2,...,a_n\} \)

A subset with \(m\) elements can be formed by choosing \(m\) elements from this set of \(n\) elements.

This number is \( {}^nC_m \)

The nummber of elements of a subset can be 0,1,2,..,n.

So, number of subsets is:

\( {}^nC_0 + {}^nC_1 + {}^nC_2 + \dots + {}^nC_n = 2^n \)

data.explanation_txt:
Note that if \( X \) is of order \( m \times n \) and \(Y\) is of order \( n \times p \), the order of \( XY \) is \( m \times p \).

But since \(BC \) is not defined, (d) is not defined.

i.e. 1 gram equivalent = 50 gm

Now, Equivalent weight of metal = Equivalent weight of metal carbonate - Equivalent weight of metal = 50 gm - 30 gm = 20 gm

data.question_title: Which of the following should be done in order to prepare 0.40M -NaCl starting with 100ml of 0.30M NaCl? (Mol.wt. of NaCl = 58.5)
data.explanation_txt:
The given solution is of concentration 0.3M so to increase the concentration one has to either evaporate the excess water or add an extra amount of NaCl to the solution.

Amount of NaCl to be added = 100 ml of 0.1N NaCl = 0.1*0.1 gram equivalent = 0.01 gram equivalent = 0.01 moles

Amount of water to be evaporated can be calculated as

100 ml of 0.3 N NaCl = 75 ml of 0.4N NaCl

\(\therefore\) Either 0.01 moles of NaCl should be added or 25 ml of water should be evaporated.

No. of gram equivalent of HCl reacted = 0.1*0.1 = 0.01

Amount of CaCO\(_3\) present in the mixture = No. of gram equivalent \(\times\) Equivalent Weight = 0.01*50 = 0.5 gm

The percentage of CaCO\(_3\) = \(\cfrac{0.5}{1} \times 100 \%\) = 50%

data.question_title:
A vexed problem facing us is the clamor to open more colleges and to reserve more seats for backward classes. But it will be a sheer folly to expand such facilities recklessly without giving any thought to the quality education imparted. If admissions are made far more selective, it will automatically reduce the number of entrants. This should apply particularly to new colleges, many of which are little more than degree factories. Only then can the authorities know how to bring down the teacher-student ratio to manageable proportions. What is more, teachers should be given refresher courses every summer to brush up their knowledge. Besides if the college management increases their library budget it will help both the staff and the students a great deal.

At the same time, however, it will be unfair to deny college education to thousands of young men and women, unless employers stop insisting on degrees even for clerical jobs. For a start, why cannot the government disqualify graduates from securing certain jobs, say Class III and IV posts? Once the link between degrees and jobs is severed, at least in some important departments, it will make young people think twice before joining college.
